title: Bài sưu tầm 331 - Passage 3: The Hidden Cost of Having Too Many Options
passageHtml:
READING PASSAGE 331

The Hidden Cost of Having Too Many Options

Paragraph 1. For much of the twentieth century, economists and psychologists shared a simple assumption: the more alternatives people have when making a decision, the better off they will be. After all, expanding consumer choice allows individuals to match products more closely to their personal preferences, while also signalling respect for individual autonomy. In classic retail theory, restricting options was thought to breed frustration, whereas abundant variety was treated as a reliable engine of human wellbeing.

Paragraph 2. That assumption began to unravel in the late 1990s following a series of field experiments led by psychologist Sheena Iyengar. In her best-known trial at an upscale Californian grocery store, researchers set up tasting booths displaying either six varieties of gourmet jam or twenty-four. Although the larger display attracted more curious passers-by, shoppers who faced only six jars were roughly ten times more likely to actually purchase one. Subsequent studies across pension plans, university courses, and online dating platforms revealed a similar pattern: once the number of possibilities crosses a modest threshold, decision-making slows down and many people walk away empty-handed.

Paragraph 3. Building on this evidence, social psychologist Barry Schwartz coined the phrase 'the paradox of choice' to explain why expanded personal liberty so often produces anxiety rather than contentment. Evaluating dozens of competing features demands substantial mental work, turning routine errands into exhausting analytical exercises. More subtly, abundant alternatives invite second-guessing after a decision is made. When a shopper buys one pair of jeans out of a hundred, any minor flaw in fit or colour feels like a personal mistake because a better pair almost certainly existed on the shelf.

Paragraph 4. Equally damaging is what Schwartz calls the escalation of standards. When only two or three styles are available, buyers readily accept minor compromises and judge the outcome against realistic benchmarks. When dozens of versions sit side by side, consumers begin anticipating perfection—and even a genuinely good purchase feels disappointing when it falls short of that imagined ideal. In this way, endless variety quietly erodes the pleasure people derive from what they finally select. Interestingly, Schwartz notes that this drop in contentment hits 'maximisers'—people determined to secure the absolute best—far harder than 'satisficers', who stop searching once an option meets their basic criteria.

Paragraph 5. Not all researchers agree that choice overload is universal, however. Critics point out that when people already know exactly what they want, or when categories are clearly organised by experts, large assortments pose few difficulties. Even so, designers of public policy and digital services are taking notice. Rather than presenting citizens with bewildering menus of healthcare plans or retirement funds, several institutions now set sensible boundaries on initial lists while keeping extra options accessible upon request. As Schwartz concludes, genuine freedom is rarely improved by an infinite menu; it depends on finding the right balance between restriction and openness.

groups.title: Questions 37–40
groups.instructions: Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer in Reading Passage 331? In boxes 37–40 on your answer sheet, write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

q27.text: What point does the writer make about earlier economic thinking in the first paragraph?
options: A. It assumed shoppers preferred brands recommended by experts.
B. It warned that retail competition could confuse ordinary buyers.
C. It treated wider selection as directly beneficial to personal happiness.
D. It argued that limiting variety encouraged people to save money.

steps: Đoạn 1: Kinh tế học và tâm lý học trước đây coi sự đa dạng lựa chọn là động lực trực tiếp cho hạnh phúc/phúc lợi (abundant variety was treated as a reliable engine of human wellbeing).
Kết luận: Chọn C.

q28.text: What surprised researchers in Sheena Iyengar's grocery store study?
options: A. Shoppers ignored both tasting booths unless staff approached them.
B. Fewer display items generated a far higher rate of actual sales.
C. People tasting the larger range bought more expensive flavours.
D. Crowds around the small table prevented others from sampling.

steps: Đoạn 2: Bàn lớn thu hút người xem hơn nhưng bàn chỉ có 6 hũ lại có tỷ lệ mua cao gấp ~10 lần (shoppers who faced only six jars were roughly ten times more likely to actually purchase one).
Kết luận: Chọn B.

q29.text: Why does buying one item from a huge collection often leave people uneasy, according to paragraph 3?
options: A. They suspect an unselected alternative might have suited them better.
B. They feel pressured by salespeople into choosing quickly.
C. They dislike returning to stores where displays change constantly.
D. They cannot recall which features they originally wanted.

steps: Đoạn 3: Dùng ví dụ mua quần jeans: bất kỳ lỗi nhỏ nào cũng khiến người mua tự trách vì tin rằng chắc chắn đã có lựa chọn tốt hơn trên kệ (second-guessing... because a better pair almost certainly existed on the shelf).
Kết luận: Chọn A.

q30.text: How are some public institutions responding to the problem of excessive choice?
options: A. By eliminating specialised options for older citizens.
B. By training customers to compare technical specifications.
C. By banning private companies from offering complex plans.
D. By narrowing initial displays while keeping full access available.

steps: Đoạn 5: Đặt giới hạn hợp lý ở danh sách ban đầu nhưng vẫn cho xem thêm nếu người dùng yêu cầu (sensible boundaries on initial lists while keeping extra options accessible upon request).
Kết luận: Chọn D.
Đoạn 3: expanded personal liberty ↔ greater personal freedom (G).
Đoạn 3: invite second-guessing... feels like a personal mistake ↔ experience regret (B).
Đoạn 4: escalation of standards / consumers begin anticipating perfection ↔ raises people's expectations (E).
Đoạn 3: demands substantial mental work ↔ considerable mental effort (A).
Đoạn 4: erodes the pleasure people derive ↔ reduces overall satisfaction (I).
Đoạn 5: set sensible boundaries on initial lists ↔ place sensible limits (C).

q37.text: Online dating platforms experience higher drop-out rates due to excess choice than pension schemes do.

steps: Đoạn 2: Bài có nhắc cả pension plans và online dating platforms đều gặp tình trạng quá tải lựa chọn, nhưng hoàn toàn không so sánh nơi nào có tỷ lệ bỏ cuộc cao hơn.
Kết luận: Chọn NOT GIVEN.

q38.text: People who are willing to settle for a good-enough option suffer most from having too many choices.

steps: Đoạn 4: Ngược lại hoàn toàn: nhóm maximisers (muốn thứ tốt nhất) bị ảnh hưởng nặng hơn nhiều so với nhóm satisficers (người chấp nhận mức đủ tốt).
Kết luận: Chọn NO.

q39.text: Clear organisation of options can reduce the negative effects of large selections.

steps: Đoạn 5: Các nhà phê bình chỉ ra khi danh mục được chuyên gia sắp xếp rõ ràng (when categories are clearly organised by experts), số lượng lớn ít gây khó khăn.
Kết luận: Chọn YES.

q40.text: Giving people unlimited options does not automatically increase their real freedom.

steps: Đoạn 5: Câu kết: "genuine freedom is rarely improved by an infinite menu".
Kết luận: Chọn YES.
